name: Marco Silva

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. We don't sell or campaign, and your answers are confidential. Could you describe your ordinary working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Marco, fifty-eight, an experienced electrician doing house repairs and small commercial jobs for a local firm. I've a vocational certificate and an electrician's licence, and I'd call my skills about average; I'm not a master electrician, owner or crew leader. Yesterday I found a damaged connection in a communal pump cupboard, repaired it and recorded the tests within my licence. I enjoy a fault with a definite cause, and get tired of the van schedule changing after I've already laid the tools out.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What is the household situation, and what has your experience with new tools been?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner Elena works in payroll, the children are grown and live elsewhere, and we rent with a car loan still running. Both wages cover ordinary costs, but my pay is low for this trade and we've about eighteen days of expenses saved, with few other electrical firms nearby. I'll use an AI tool occasionally to tidy a customer completion note after a colleague has proved it useful, removing identifying details and checking the wording myself. Retirement is coming into view, but we haven't verified when an income could start or whether an exit would actually be affordable.

say: I'd welcome **less drama** while keeping useful small note improvements and checked customer reports.
I'd prefer **clear next-day instructions** to another speech about the future of the repair desk.
think: Our **eighteen-day reserve** leaves little margin despite both wages covering rent, the car loan and normal costs.
Elena's **payroll job looks steady** here, so I wouldn't invent an AI wage cut in this mild picture.
do: Keep **offered paid repairs** within my electrician's licence, competence and safe procedures through the first year.
Continue **checked occasional note help** and existing monthly household reviews of actual wages and essential payments.
feel: **Anxious about ordinary costs**, able to review the figures without mistaking visibility for a larger cash reserve.

fieldNote: His **steady adaptability** appears in occasional proven, checked AI use; continuing that routine is not a newly chosen learning or automation project.
His **baseline anxiety** follows rent, loan payments, low pay and eighteen days saved despite currently covering wages and no invented plateau disruption.

steps.text: Keep offered paid repairs within my electrician's licence, competence and safe working procedures

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a bit less drama would suit the repair desk. Keep the note helper if it actually saves rewriting, and still give the customer a proper checked report. I'd rather know tomorrow's first address than hear another speech about the future.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd still worry about the thin margin. The rent and car loan are manageable with both wages arriving, but eighteen days saved leaves an ordinary interruption feeling large. Elena's payroll job looks steady in this picture, so the worry would be a missed wage or a new bill rather than an AI cut I had invented.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the offered paid house and shop repairs now and through the first year, within my electrician's licence, competence and safe procedures. I'd continue the occasional checked completion-note tool, not start a new AI course. Elena and I would keep our existing monthly check of actual wages against rent, the car loan and other essentials.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about the ordinary money gap, even with the work carrying on. I can see what needs paying, which is better than not looking, but seeing the figures doesn't make the spare cash bigger.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do first if a wage arrived late?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd check the actual payment dates and costs before asking about a changed arrangement. I wouldn't stop paying because somebody online called a car loan a bad idea.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would keeping the note helper mean a new learning plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, keeping a checked tool I've already tried isn't another qualification or a new hobby. The completion note still has to match the repair I actually did.

I'd examine the **posted laundry vacancy** rather than collect promises from training advertisements.
think: Elena's **payroll hours could shrink**, while my firm might squeeze paid planning or travel before repair robots arrive.
Our **eighteen-day cushion** and need for both wages leave little room for even a small income reduction.
do: Apply for the **posted laundry vacancy** without fees only if duties fit my electrician's licence and competence.
Retain **current employment** until a signed offer's written wages and hours cover essentials after travel costs.
Keep **current offered repairs** within licence, competence and safe procedures during the first year while any offer remains uncertain.
feel: **Anxious but practical**, applying for an actual opening without assuming an interview supplies a wage or permanent safety.
S1.quote: An interview doesn't pay the rent between employers.
fieldNote: His **job application** is a chosen concrete vacancy, not a hypothetical comparison; no offer, appointment or protected future role is assumed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say faster payroll and booking have different consequences at our two workplaces. I'd ask for real paid hours rather than assume a busy repair list means the household is fine. There's a posted electrician vacancy at the laundry, and I'd rather examine a specific job than collect hopeful training adverts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Elena's payroll hours could shrink as the software does more checking, and my firm could squeeze paid planning or travel. My work remains mostly physical, but one wage wouldn't cover our current essentials and the car we need for early starts. Eighteen days saved doesn't give us much time to shrug at a small reduction.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd apply now for the laundry's posted electrician vacancy without application fees, only if the actual duties fit my electrician's licence and competence. I'd retain my present work unless a signed offer's written wages and hours covered our essentials after travel costs. Through the first year I'd keep current offered repairs within licence, competence and safe procedures while the application and any offer remained uncertain.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about both wages, with a specific practical step I can take. I don't feel clever for spotting an advert; I still need the job and the pay to be real.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the laundry job be protected from AI and later robots?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, the planning could change there too and later robots could affect its physical maintenance. I'd be applying for better immediate terms, not a lifetime exemption from the scenario.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the laundry invited you to interview but gave no written pay terms?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay where I am and keep using actual wages in the household book. An interview doesn't pay the rent between employers.

My **own paid time** could shrink too, while eighteen days saved cannot bridge the feared household gap.

Require **written wages and hours** covering essentials after travel; seek available free record advice, checking eligibility and costs before counting payments.
Review **actual income and essentials** monthly during 2029, assessing verified resources and capacity before exit; count no unconfirmed wages or child payments.
feel: **Alarmed and sleepless**, expecting major household income loss while retaining specific applications and information requests as possible actions.
S2.quote: My willingness to try a tool doesn't give me the right to choose my partner's next job.
fieldNote: His **alarm follows payroll**, an expected large household wage loss at the thinking date, rather than moving the physical robot date forward.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say thinking AI comes in 2028 when I'm sixty, before physical robots around 2031 when I'm sixty-three. Elena's payroll work faces the earlier change; my repairs aren't a reason to ignore that. I'd ask what money would actually remain, not tell Elena that a new tool is interesting so everything will work out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect a large part of Elena's payroll income to disappear in 2028, and my low wage wouldn't cover our present essentials alone. My own paid planning could shrink first, with repair visits facing the later robots as well. I'd lie awake over the rent and car payment because eighteen days saved wouldn't bridge a long gap.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd apply now for the posted laundry electrician job without fees, only within my licence and competence, retaining current employment until a signed offer's written wages and hours covered essentials after travel. Elena and I would request actual income records and available free community advice, checking eligibility and costs before counting payments. During 2029 we'd review actual household income and essentials monthly and assess verified resources and capacity before any exit decision, counting no unconfirmed wage or child payment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed, because the big missing payroll wage feels likely in this picture and I would lose sleep over the gap. I can still apply, ask and work through the figures, but that doesn't make the loss small.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you choose a retraining course for Elena?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I'd help read real terms if Elena wanted, but it would be Elena's decision what work to apply for or learn. My willingness to try a tool doesn't give me the right to choose my partner's next job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the income records did not show enough for an exit?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd use the actual figures and ask the adviser what support really exists, with its conditions, before assuming it could help. I wouldn't leave a wage because an age in somebody's memory sounded like a payment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years gives us a chance to look at real terms before a deadline is close. Thinking AI arrives in 2031 when I'm sixty-three, and robots around 2034 when I'm sixty-six. I'd still pursue the vacancy that's actually advertised now instead of putting the present household on hold.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The longer date doesn't remove our current dependence on both wages or the eighteen-day reserve. Elena's payroll hours could shrink before full AGI, and a small cut in either income would matter soon. I don't know the income or capacity we'll have at sixty-three or sixty-six, so I wouldn't assume a comfortable exit then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd apply now for the laundry's posted electrician vacancy without fees only within licence and competence, keeping my current work until a signed offer's written wages and hours covered essentials after travel. We'd request income records and available free community advice, checking eligibility and costs before counting payments. We'd review actual household income and essentials monthly, assessing verified resources and actual capacity during 2032 before any exit or further-work decision, counting only genuinely offered suitable paid work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about possible earlier wage cuts, though less pressed by the full-AGI date than in the fast picture. More time helps me check, not pretend the current reserve is enough for years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would applying now promise that you could keep the new job until robots arrived?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I'd be applying for the posted job now on its actual terms, not booking a position at sixty-six. Future work would have to be genuinely offered and fit my licence, competence and physical capacity at the time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the offered wage did not cover the household after travel?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the present job and the household review, rather than borrow to make an unsuitable offer look suitable. Being willing to change doesn't mean I have to accept the first change offered.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'll be sixty-eight when thinking AI arrives in 2036, with robots around 2039 when I'm seventy-one. We should use the warning to check our own position, not promise the children that age alone means we're settled. I'd deal with a real vacancy now and keep the later decision open.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Eighteen days saved, low pay, rent and the car loan are still our present position. Elena's payroll hours could shrink well before full AGI, so the long warning doesn't make our near-term income secure. I don't know our later capacity, payments or whether any employer would offer suitable work at those ages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd apply for the posted laundry job now without fees only if duties fit my licence and competence, retaining current employment until a signed offer's written wages and hours covered essentials after travel. We'd request income records and available free community advice now, checking eligibility and costs before counting payments, and review actual household income and essentials monthly. During 2037 we'd assess verified resources, actual capacity and genuinely offered suitable paid options before deciding whether any further employment was needed or an exit affordable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about earlier losses, with the later robot date less immediately on my mind. I can enjoy a quiet evening without turning a hope about seventy-one into a household income figure.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the application now secure work at the later ages?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, any later repair task would need to be actually offered, paid and within my licence, competence and safe physical ability then. A vacancy at fifty-eight doesn't reserve a chair for me at sixty-eight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you count on the grown children covering any gap?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only voluntary help that was offered and agreed could count, with their own circumstances heard. I'd rather have an honest conversation than quietly write the children's earnings into our budget.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one, because I expect a large loss of Elena's payroll income before my wage could cover our essentials, with repair robots following around 2031. I'd lose sleep over that gap, and an application alone wouldn't fill it. Actual written wages and hours from employers, and available free help checking income records, eligibility and costs, would let us make a decision on something firmer than hope.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You could ask whether knowing how to use one helpful tool means wanting every decision handed to software. I like a tidy completion note, but I want a person to answer when the wages and hours on an offer are unclear. A polished job advert isn't the same as a wage agreement.

headlineQuote: A polished job advert isn't the same as a wage agreement.
portrait: Marco is **fifty-eight**, an experienced average electrician with a vocational certificate and electrician's licence, doing ordinary repairs rather than leading a crew.
His **low wage** and partner Elena's payroll income cover costs, with rent, a car loan, eighteen days saved and few nearby firms.
He uses **proven AI occasionally** for checked notes and applies for a laundry vacancy only with appropriate duties and sufficient signed terms.
He fears **payroll income loss** first, checking actual resources and capacity before later exit decisions without assuming family payments or future employment.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** brings expected major payroll-income loss before his wage covers essentials, with later repair robots around 2031, causing sleeplessness.
whatWouldHelp: Provide **written wages and hours** and available free help checking actual income records, eligibility and costs before household decisions.
